refibra.origin: REFIBRA is a Lenzing AG technology name, not a fiber. It denotes Lenzing's route for converting cotton scraps into pulp that is blended with wood pulp and spun into TENCEL lyocell, and later into LENZING ECOVERO viscose. The generic fiber in a REFIBRA product is therefore lyocell or viscose. Lenzing describes the cotton inputs as pre-consumer offcuts from garment making and, increasingly, post-consumer cotton textiles.
refibra.structure: The finished fiber is regenerated cellulose (cellulose II) indistinguishable in chemistry from lyocell or viscose made only from wood. Cotton cellulose has a high degree of polymerization, but the pulping step shortens and purifies the chains to a range suitable for dissolution. What changes is the feedstock history, not the polymer. Residual dyes, finishes and non-cellulosic fibers such as polyester or elastane in the waste must be removed, because they would contaminate the spinning dope and weaken or discolor the fiber.
refibra.process: As Lenzing describes it, cotton scraps are sorted, mechanically opened and chemically treated in a pulping step to remove dyes and other contaminants and produce a cellulose pulp. This recycled pulp is mixed with wood pulp and processed in the ordinary lyocell (NMMO direct dissolution) or viscose route. Lenzing states that production began in 2017 with about 20% recycled cotton pulp, later raised to about 30% combined pre- and post-consumer material, with the balance from wood. The share varies by product and should be confirmed for each lot.
refibra.performance: Performance follows the underlying fiber: REFIBRA lyocell behaves like lyocell (good wet strength, moisture regain roughly 11%, fibrillation under wet abrasion) and REFIBRA viscose behaves like viscose. Lenzing presents the recycled content as not reducing quality at the stated blend levels. Because recycled cotton pulp and wood pulp are co-processed, any difference in dyeing, strength or hand should be judged by testing the actual yarn rather than assumed from the technology name.
refibra.identify: No burn, microscopy or FTIR test can separate REFIBRA fiber from standard lyocell or viscose, since the polymer is identical. Burn behavior is that of cellulose (indicative only). Buyers should verify recycled content through transaction certificates and producer documentation. A common error is treating REFIBRA as a separate fiber type on a label.
refibra.labeling: REFIBRA is a technology trademark and cannot replace the generic name. In the US, labels must state lyocell (a subclass of rayon) or rayon under the TFPIA and 16 CFR Part 303; in the EU, lyocell or viscose under Regulation (EU) No 1007/2011. Recycled-content statements are marketing claims that must be substantiated; any third-party recycled-content certification should be confirmed by certificate scope rather than assumed from the brand.
refibra.past: Lenzing introduced REFIBRA in 2017, describing TENCEL x REFIBRA as among the first commercially available cellulose fibers with chemically recycled content. The company first used post-industrial cutting waste, then increased the recycled share and began incorporating post-consumer cotton. It later extended the technology to ECOVERO viscose. REFIBRA emerged alongside other textile-to-textile cellulose efforts in Northern Europe, such as Renewcell's CIRCULOSE pulp, reflecting efforts to reduce wood demand and landfill of cotton waste.

econyl.origin: ECONYL is a trademark of the Aquafil Group, headquartered in Arco, Italy. The underlying generic fiber is nylon 6 (polyamide 6), regenerated from nylon waste. Aquafil states that its depolymerization and repolymerization take place at its site in Ljubljana, Slovenia, which has hosted the ECONYL regeneration system since 2011. Aquafil lists inputs such as discarded fishing nets, carpet face fiber and industrial nylon scrap; the mix varies by product and period.
econyl.structure: Nylon 6 is an aliphatic polyamide built from a single monomer, epsilon-caprolactam, which ring-opens so that each repeat unit contains five methylene groups and one amide linkage. Hydrogen bonds between amide groups on neighboring chains give nylon its strength, toughness and moderate moisture absorption. ECONYL is chemically identical to virgin nylon 6 because it is rebuilt from purified caprolactam. Filament cross-sections are usually round, and properties are set by drawing, texturing and polymer grade rather than by the waste source.
econyl.process: Aquafil describes the ECONYL Regeneration System as follows: nylon waste is collected, sorted and cleaned, and non-nylon components are separated. The nylon enters a chemical depolymerization in which steam, heat and a catalyst break the polymer back to caprolactam, which is vaporized, condensed and purified in distillation columns. The purified monomer is repolymerized into nylon 6, which is melt-spun into textile filament yarn (and into carpet yarn). Aquafil publishes Environmental Product Declarations for ECONYL yarns covering its own life-cycle claims.
econyl.performance: ECONYL performs as nylon 6: high tenacity and abrasion resistance, good elastic recovery at low strain, and moisture regain of a few percent, higher than polyester. It is thermoplastic and softens and melts on heating, so ironing temperature matters. Acid dyes bind to terminal amine groups, and disperse dyes can also be used. Nylon yellows and loses strength under prolonged UV exposure unless stabilized. Aquafil's claim that ECONYL matches virgin nylon quality refers to its purified monomer route.
econyl.identify: Burn tests are indicative only: nylon melts and shrinks from flame, burns with a celery-like odor and leaves a hard bead. FTIR identifies polyamide and differential scanning calorimetry separates nylon 6 from nylon 6,6 by melting point. No lab test distinguishes ECONYL from virgin nylon 6. A frequent overstatement is that all ECONYL comes from ocean fishing nets; Aquafil itself lists several waste streams.
econyl.labeling: ECONYL is a trademark, not a generic name. US labels must use nylon under the TFPIA and 16 CFR Part 303, and EU labels polyamide or nylon under Regulation (EU) No 1007/2011. Recycled or regenerated content claims must be substantiated; buyers can ask for Aquafil's published EPDs and for any third-party recycled-content certificate covering the specific yarn. The brand name alone does not establish the recycled share of a finished fabric.
econyl.past: Aquafil, founded as a nylon yarn maker in Italy, expanded into Slovenia in the mid-1990s through the privatization of a former state company. It experimented with nylon recycling in the 1990s and from 2007 pursued a full waste-to-yarn loop, launching the ECONYL regeneration system in 2011. The brand gained visibility through fashion and swimwear collaborations and through campaigns linking fishing-net recovery to marine conservation. Nylon 6 lends itself to this route because, unlike many polymers, it depolymerizes cleanly back to a single monomer.
